source.title: Towards Understanding Generalization in DP-GD: A Case Study in Training Two-Layer CNNs
source.authors: Zhongjie Shi; Pu-Yu Wang; Chen-Yang Zhang; Yuan Cao

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices. The displayed arXiv version/date and the supplied venue/year metadata are inconsistent; retained as supplied.
record.tranche_reason: Reports theoretical and empirical generalization results for two-layer CNNs on a constructed signal-plus-noise classification task, extending the generalization topic to private gradient training. It does not test the specific behaviors in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper tests GD and DP-GD generalization on synthetic data with label-dependent signals and label-independent noise. It does not use arbitrary or random labels. The empirical figure results are described in the text; cited studies are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: The study compares GD and differentially private GD on a constructed signal-plus-noise task. Its results test none of V1–V8. Labels are sampled randomly but determine an input signal, so this is not V1's experiment with labels independent of inputs.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: on the constructed task, both methods can attain arbitrarily small training loss, while suitably configured, early-stopped DP-GD can generalize better than GD and provide privacy guarantees. Training-loss convergence and the early-stopped test-error guarantee concern different iterates.
record.recipe_differences: Studies differentially private gradient perturbation and early stopping on a constructed binary classification task; it does not reproduce the original claim's random-label experiments or its listed benchmark studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Signal-to-noise ratio changes the relative test performance in the numerical experiments. The theory's conclusions depend on stated SNR, initialization, learning-rate, noise, and early-stopping conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Condition 1, GD attains arbitrarily small training loss while test loss remains at least 0.1; with an additional initialization bound, test error is at least 0.11. Under Condition 2 and selected noise and stopping parameters, DP-GD has test error at most 0.01. Experiments show similar performance at noise 0.1 and DP-GD advantages at noise 0.3 and 0.5, including 95% versus 75% accuracy at 0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On a constructed binary classification task using two-layer Huberized ReLU CNNs, suitably configured gradient noise and early stopping can improve generalization relative to GD.

record.peer_reviewed: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (as supplied)
record.problems: The theoretical conclusions apply to a specially constructed distribution and restrictive assumptions. Numerical experiments use one two-layer CNN setup and three noise levels; text reports no uncertainty estimates for these plotted results.

untested.parts: Independent fixed random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label training and held-out random-label accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects, including dependence on training-set size and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing measures. Injecting gradient noise does not measure weight-perturbation tolerance.
Retraining after removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: T3 requires a result on a claim version; a new generalization setting alone is insufficient. All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, without disputing the reported results. The theoretical GD and DP-GD guarantees have different initialization and hyperparameter conditions.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fitting fixed random labels, natural-label generalization, or chance accuracy on held-out random labels.
No width sweep or comparison beyond the width needed for zero training error.
No fully connected network comparator or test of local connectivity.
No batch-size comparison or fixed-epoch batch experiment.
No sharpness, perturbation tolerance, norm, or margin measurement.
No removal of memorized examples or retraining comparison.
